title: The Elegance of a Stupid Question - Nautilus
gist: Nautilus traces the cannonball-stacking question Sir Walter Raleigh put to his mathematical assistant Thomas Harriot — a practical shipboard logistics problem — and asks whether computers in mathematics are rewriting what counts as a stupid or smart question.

insights.claim: Sir Walter Raleigh asked his mathematical assistant Thomas Harriot whether there was a formula for the number of cannonballs in regularly stacked piles — the seemingly stupid question that opened the sphere-packing problem.
insights.so_what: Operational logistics questions have repeatedly generated centuries of durable intellectual output — a case for taking mundane constraint problems seriously as research seeds.
insights.quote: Cannonballs, Raleigh asked his mathematical assistant Thomas Harriot: How many per stack?
insights.locator: Cannonballs, Raleigh asked his mathematical assistant
insights.speaker: Jason Socrates Bardi

insights.claim: The cannonball question was immensely practical because space below-decks on a British merchant ship or man-o-war was at a premium, making stacking efficiency a real commercial and military constraint.
insights.so_what: Packing efficiency under a hard volume constraint is the same optimization that governs modern container shipping and datacenter density.
insights.quote: an immensely practical question, since space below-decks on a British merchant ship or man-o-war was at a premium
insights.locator: Raleigh wanted to know if there was a formula
insights.speaker: Jason Socrates Bardi

insights.claim: Raleigh raised the question while preparing an expedition to South America to search for a mythical city of gold and bring its riches back to London, tying the mathematics to a speculative resource venture.
insights.so_what: Speculative resource ventures have historically funded incidental technical advances that outlast the venture itself.
insights.locator: He was gearing up to lead an expedition to South America
insights.speaker: Jason Socrates Bardi

insights.claim: The piece asks whether the arrival of computers in mathematics is rewriting the definitions of stupid and smart questions.
insights.so_what: If machine proof-checking makes brute-force-tractable questions valuable, the premium shifts from elegance to formulability — a change in what mathematical talent is worth.
insights.quote: Are computers in mathematics rewriting the definitions of stupid and smart?
insights.locator: The Elegance of a Stupid Question
insights.speaker: Jason Socrates Bardi
